note: The DAK component layer. DAK.fsh declares NINE components and this layer carries all of them -- eight as classes here, and healthInterventions as l1:health-intervention, which L1 already declares as its hinge to L2 -- plus a TENTH, scheduling-logic, which DAK.fsh omits and the published SOP treats as an active L2 input. The internals of BPMN and DMN files are NOT here: they are separate subgraphs, l2-bpmn and l2-dmn, because a DAK component points at a file by URI and what is inside that file is a different question with a different vocabulary, a different extractor and a different failure mode. This layer also carries the L1->L2 hop, because l1 cannot name an l2 class without a circular import.

groundedIn.detail: "Logical Model for representing a complete Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) with metadata and all 9 DAK components": healthInterventions, personas, userScenarios, businessProcesses, dataElements, decisionLogic, indicators, requirements, testScenarios. Each is `0..* <Component>Source`. The class list below is that list, not a subset of it.

groundedIn.what: The uniform source pattern every component uses
groundedIn.detail: Nine parallel Source types, each offering exactly one of `url`, `canonical` or an inline `instance`. A component is therefore reachable three different ways, and `sourceKind` on each class below records which was used -- a canonical reference and a raw URL do not carry the same guarantees and flattening them would hide that.

Carries id, name, title, version, status, publicationUrl, previewUrl, canonicalUrl, license, copyrightYear and publisher -- and none of the nine component arrays, because smart-base defines the model rather than instantiating a DAK. The `dak` class records exactly the metadata that file carries.

SGRequirements instances carrying 170 statements (155 SHALL, 15 SHOULD) and 47 actor references across 10 personas, each written as `actor[+] = Canonical(SGAuthoring.Persona.X)`. This is the richest structured content in the repository and the one place a DAK component references another BY CANONICAL rather than by name.

groundedIn.what: The three id-reference joins the model declares
groundedIn.detail: `scenario 0..* id` ("References to user scenario IDs"), `personas 0..* id` ("References to persona IDs"), and `references 0..* id` ("References to Health Intervention IDs"). All three are bare id strings with no declared target profile -- resolvable only by matching against the ids of instances that may or may not exist.

groundedIn.what: The published SOP's L2 content types, which do not match DAK.fsh's nine
groundedIn.detail: The SOP's "Input for authoring L3" table lists ten content types: Health Interventions, Generic Personas, User Scenarios, Processes, Data Elements, Decision Tables, Scheduling Logic, Indicators, Functional Requirements, Non-functional Requirements. DAK.fsh lists nine and they are not the same nine -- it has testScenarios and a single combined requirements component, and no Scheduling Logic. This layer keeps DAK.fsh's list because that is the machine-readable model the extractor reads, and adds scheduling-logic because the SOP treats it as an active L2 input, WHO's ArchiMate model declares it a BusinessObject, and l1:schedule-entry otherwise has nowhere to land. The divergence is recorded here rather than silently reconciled; it is a question for the technical working group, not for this repository.

predicates.note: A DAK contains one of its nine components. The qualifier carries the component name from DAK.fsh, so `dak hasComponent persona` and `dak hasComponent program-indicator` stay distinguishable when a query walks the kit.

A component points at the file that defines it. TWO TARGETS ARE LICENSED, and which one an instance uses says how much is known about the file. Where a subgraph models that file type, the target is the file itself -- `business-process sourcedFrom bpmn-definitions`, licensed in l2-bpmn -- and the graph walks straight on into the file's contents. Where none does (a Gherkin feature, a FHIR canonical, or a BPMN this graph simply does not hold), the target is an l1:external-artifact carrying a URI and nothing else. Prefer the first: routing through external-artifact when the file IS modelled adds a hop through a node that, at instance level, is the same node.
A business process realises a user scenario. From `scenario 0..* id` on BusinessProcessWorkflow -- a bare id string, so an instance carries a resolutionStatus.
A user scenario involves a persona. From `personas 0..* id` on UserScenario -- again bare ids, again a resolutionStatus.

A functional requirement is fulfilled by a persona. THE ONE JOIN IN THIS LAYER THAT IS NOT STRING MATCHING: the committed instances write `actor[+] = Canonical(SGAuthoring.Persona.BusinessAnalyst)`, a canonical reference that resolves without guessing. It is the counter-example that shows the other joins are a choice, not a necessity.
A requirement carries numbered, labelled statements with a conformance verb. 170 of them exist today.

BusinessProcessWorkflow declares `task 0..*` with identifier, name and description -- the same tasks the BPMN file draws. Two representations of one list, joined by identifier, which is why dak-task exists as a node rather than a property.

A program indicator names the health interventions that give it context. From `references 0..* id` on ProgramIndicator -- bare id strings again, so an instance carries a resolutionStatus. Distinct from derivedFrom: referencing an intervention for context is not the same claim as restating a normative indicator.
A DAK-level task entry describes an element of a BPMN file. Declared here and licensed in l2-bpmn, where the target class lives.

Reused from l1, and licensed here for the L1->L2 hop that L1 could not declare itself: l1 cannot name an l2 class without a circular import, but l2 imports l1 and sees both ends. A recommendation is implemented by the DAK component that realises it. Always `inferred`, never `derived` -- deciding that a process realises a recommendation is adaptation, the judgement a DAK exists to record, and it carries a resolutionStatus like every other cross-artefact claim. Note health-intervention has NO implementedBy edge: the published SOP gives Health Interventions an L3 row of `n/a / n/a / n/a` and calls L1 recommendations inputs rather than outputs, so the trace runs through processes, decisions and indicators instead.

classes.name: Digital Adaptation Kit
classes.note: The kit itself. Properties are exactly the metadata fields DAK.fsh declares and dak.json carries -- no more, so that a dak node can be produced from a real file without anything being invented.
classes.propertyNote: canonicalUrl equals publicationUrl on a release branch and previewUrl on a development branch, per DAK.fsh. Both are kept because which one canonicalUrl currently equals is what says whether a graph describes a release or a build.

classes.name: Generic Persona
classes.note: DAK component 2. Grounded in GenericPersona.fsh -- title, id, description, otherNames, iscoCode bound to ISCO08ValueSet -- and in the 22 committed ActorDefinition instances that carry name, title, type and description. The two disagree about where ISCO lives, which the properties record rather than smooth over.
classes.propertyNote: `title` is the human-readable label a BPMN pool matches on; `name` is the CamelCase identifier a Canonical() reference matches on. They are different strings for the same persona and conflating them is precisely how the pool join breaks. GenericPersona.fsh declares `iscoCode 0..* code`, but the committed ActorDefinitions record ISCO in prose inside description, so iscoCode is usually empty and is not authoritative.

classes.name: User Scenario
classes.note: DAK component 3. A narrative describing how personas interact. Carries `personas 0..* id`, which is the only structured link between the narrative layer and the personas it names.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Business Process Workflow
classes.note: DAK component 4. NOT the BPMN file -- the component that points at one. `source 1..1 uri` is that pointer, and the BPMN's interior is the l2-bpmn subgraph, reached through the external-artifact this sourcedFrom targets.
classes.propertyNote: `objectives 1..1 markdown` is required by BusinessProcessWorkflow.fsh and has no counterpart anywhere in BPMN XML, so it can only ever come from the FSH instance. resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Task Entry
classes.note: One entry of BusinessProcessWorkflow's `task 0..*` backbone: identifier, name, description. A node rather than a property because the same task is also drawn in the BPMN file, and the two lists have to be joinable to be checkable against each other.

classes.name: Core Data Element
classes.note: DAK component 5. CoreDataElement.fsh calls itself "the ONE EXCEPTION to allowing FHIR R4 models into the DAK LMs": `type` is one of valueset | codesystem | conceptmap | logicalmodel and `canonical 1..1 uri` points at it. The canonical is recorded; nothing inside it is copied, because FHIR is its own query layer.
classes.propertyNote: `name`, `resolutionStatus` and `extractionRule` are for elements recovered from DMN input expressions rather than declared in a dictionary. A recovered element is a name that was REFERENCED, not a definition that was found, and only a resolved one may carry a canonical.

classes.name: Decision-Support Logic
classes.note: DAK component 6. The whole model is an id, an optional description and `source 1..1 uri` to a DMN file. Nothing about the decision itself -- which is the gap the l2-dmn subgraph fills.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Scheduling Logic
classes.note: When an intervention is due, as a DAK component. NOT declared by DAK.fsh -- it is added here because the published SOP lists Scheduling Logic as an active L2 input (spreadsheets under input/scheduling-logic), WHO's ArchiMate model declares it a BusinessObject realised by PlanDefinition, and l1:schedule and l1:schedule-entry had no L2 component to reach. Note that the SOP's own L3 row for scheduling is present but HTML-commented-out and there is no l3_schedulinglogic.md page, so WHO has drafted the mapping and not activated it; the L3 edge is licensed here as a deliberate departure, recorded rather than hidden.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Program Indicator
classes.note: DAK component 7. Named program-indicator and not `indicator` because L1 already declares an `indicator` -- one normatively defined in a publication. They are different things: this is the DAK's operational measure, and `derivedFrom` is how it points at the normative one. Collapsing them would silently merge a WHO definition with a country's implementation of it.
classes.propertyNote: numerator, denominator and disaggregation are all `1..1 markdown` -- prose, not a computable expression. Nothing here should be read as a calculable measure; the L3 FHIR Measure is where that would live. resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Functional Requirement
classes.note: DAK component 8, first half. The as-a/I-want/so-that shape: `activity`, `capability[x]`, `benefit[x]`, and `actor 0..* Reference(SGActor)`. The 41 committed instances use the R5 SGRequirements profile rather than this logical model, so a real instance carries `statement` entries and a userstory extension; both shapes are accommodated and `profile` records which was read.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Non-Functional Requirement
classes.note: DAK component 8, second half. `requirement 1..1 markdown`, an optional category and classification codings. Kept separate from the functional half because the fields genuinely differ -- a non-functional requirement has no actor and no benefit.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

classes.name: Requirement Statement
classes.note: One numbered, labelled statement inside a requirement, with a conformance verb. A node rather than a property because conformance is queried across a whole DAK -- 'every SHALL in this kit, and what fulfils it' is the question requirements exist to answer.
classes.propertyNote: conformance is the FHIR ConformanceExpectation verb: SHALL, SHOULD, MAY or SHOULD-NOT. Across the 41 committed instances it is 155 SHALL and 15 SHOULD.

classes.name: Test Scenario
classes.note: DAK component 9. `feature 1..1 uri` to a Gherkin feature file, plus an optional description. The feature file's interior is not modelled: no DAK in this estate ships one yet, so a subgraph for it would have no instance to check it against.
classes.propertyNote: resolutionStatus is `unresolved` on a component that something else names but no DAK declares -- an L3 artefact whose title carries the component id, for instance. The node exists so the gap is queryable and carries the referenced id and nothing else.

deliberatelyOmitted.why: DAK component 1 is already l1:health-intervention, which L1 declares as its hinge to L2 and grounds in this same HealthInterventions.fsh. A second class for it would be two names for one thing across a layer boundary -- the exact failure the shared-IRI rule exists to prevent.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: A `derivedFrom` edge from a data element to a recommendation
deliberatelyOmitted.why: Plausible -- a dictionary entry often exists because a recommendation asks for it -- but no committed artefact records the link, and nothing in CoreDataElement.fsh provides for it. Same rule that excluded `writes` from the DMN subgraph.
The nine Source types in DAKComponentSources.fsh are one pattern repeated nine times: url, canonical, or inline instance. That is a property of the reference (`sourceKind`), not nine classes.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: The interior of BPMN and DMN files
deliberatelyOmitted.why: Separate subgraphs -- l2-bpmn and l2-dmn. A component points at a file by URI; what is inside it has its own vocabulary (OMG's, not WHO's), its own extractor and its own failure modes, and mixing the two would make the DAK component layer unreadable.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: The interior of a Gherkin feature file
deliberatelyOmitted.why: No DAK in this estate ships one. A subgraph with no instance to check it against is speculative vocabulary.

deliberatelyOmitted.what: The contents of any FHIR canonical
deliberatelyOmitted.why: ValueSets, CodeSystems, ConceptMaps and logical models have a validator, a publisher and canonical references already. Record the URL; re-represent nothing.

The published SOP's authored-L3 table gives Health Interventions `n/a` in all three columns, and the L2 guidance calls health interventions and the L1 recommendations behind them inputs rather than outputs. WHO's ArchiMate model disagrees -- it has `L3: Plan Definition realises Health Intervention` -- and that contradiction is recorded rather than resolved here. L1 reaches L3 through business-process, decision-support-logic and program-indicator instead.
